title: Centralized vs Distributed
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1a · Section 1-1 · Version control systems Centralized vs Distributed With Git, every computer holds the whole history. GitHub is a copy you share, not the only copy. Where does the history live? online Centralized Distributed (Git) Switch the mode, then click the server to take it offline. The one idea Centralized: one copy of the history, so when the server is down nobody commits. Distributed: a full copy on every computer. Git is distributed. GitHub is the copy you share; commits work offline and you push when you are back. That is why you commit on your machine first and push second.

title: Compile, Bytecode, JVM
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 2-1 · Compiling Java Compile, Bytecode, JVM javac checks it and turns it into bytecode once; a JVM on any computer runs that same bytecode. Source Focus HelloWorld.java source text javac HelloWorld.java javac the Java compiler HelloWorld.class target/classes/com/pluralsight the same .class, copied to any computer step 0 / 8 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · the source is HelloWorld.java. Try missing semicolon. HelloWorld.java .class file ? Runs on ? The one idea javac turns source into bytecode once , and only when the grammar is right. The JVM runs that bytecode anywhere : the same HelloWorld.class works on a Mac, a Windows PC and a Linux machine. A syntax error stops at javac: no .class, nothing to run .

title: JDK, JRE, JVM
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 2-1 · The Java platform JDK, JRE, JVM Three names that nest inside each other. Pick what you want to do and watch which layer lights up. One inside the other JDK Java Development Kit For writing programs. The tools a developer needs, plus a JRE inside so you can test what you wrote. javac compiler debugger javadoc jar tool JRE Java Runtime Environment For running programs. The class libraries your code calls, plus the JVM that executes it. No compiler. java.lang java.util java.io class libraries JVM Java Virtual Machine The engine. Loads a .class file and executes its bytecode. One JVM per kind of computer, so the same .class runs anywhere. class loader bytecode interpreter garbage collector you need JDK Write a Java program Run a Java program Just execute bytecode IntelliJ uses the JDK you installed, Amazon Corretto 17 . So you already have all three layers. The one idea JVM runs bytecode. JRE is the JVM plus the class libraries: enough to run. JDK is the JRE plus the tools: needed to write. Install a JDK and you get all three; install only a JRE and you can run programs but never compile one.

A declared local variable holds nothing usable until you give it a value; only fields get a default.

title: final Constants
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-1 · Read-only variables final Constants Flip final on and the line that tries to change it no longer compiles. Main.java 1 final String myName = "Raymond" ; 2 System.out.println( "Your name is: " + myName); 3 myName = myName + " Maroun" ; Cannot assign a value to final variable 'myName' 4 System.out.println( "The full name is: " + myName); The variable String myName final off final off final on A value fixed for every run is a constant, named in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE : final int DAYS_IN_WEEK = 7; The one idea final means assign once. The compiler stops any later change before the program ever runs, which is why constants like DAYS_IN_WEEK are declared final.

title: Naming Conventions
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-1 · Naming conventions and consistency Naming Conventions Click any name in the code and see what kind of thing it is and which rule shaped it. Names Real names from this week package com.pluralsight ; import java.util . Scanner ; public class Main { public static void main ( String [] args ) { final int DAYS_IN_WEEK = 7; int firstNumber = 26; boolean isEnrolled = true ; Scanner myScanner = new Scanner (System.in); String firstName = myScanner . nextLine (); String lastName = myScanner . nextLine (); String fullName = generateFullName ( firstName , lastName ); } public static int addNumbers ( int num1 , int num2 ) { return num1 + num2 ; } public static String generateFullName ( String firstName , String lastName ) { return firstName + " " + lastName ; } } The five shapes Class PascalCase Main, HelloWorld, Scanner Variable camelCase firstNumber, isEnrolled Method camelCase() addNumbers, generateFullName Constant (final) UPPER_SNAKE_CASE DAYS_IN_WEEK Package all.lowercase com.pluralsight The compiler accepts first_number or main_class . Nobody writes them, so they stand out as wrong. The one idea The shape of a name tells the reader what it is before they read the code. The compiler does not enforce these rules, but every Java developer follows them, so a name in the wrong shape reads as a mistake.

title: Concatenation vs Addition
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-2 · String concatenation Concatenation vs Addition In Java, + has two jobs. Between two numbers it adds; the moment a String is on either side, it glues text together. Pick an expression Focus How Java reads the line, one + at a time number + number → addition String + anything → concatenation step 0 / 6 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · Try all three. Main.java this + means ? result type ? console The one idea + becomes concatenation the moment a String is on either side , and Java works left to right, one + at a time. So "Sum: " + 1 + 2 prints Sum: 12, while 1 + 2 + " apples" prints 3 apples. Put parentheses around the math you want done first: "Sum: " + (1 + 2) prints Sum: 3.

title: Integer Division and Modulo
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-2 · Operators and expressions Integer Division and Modulo When both sides are int, 10 / 3 is 3: the leftover is cut off, and % hands that leftover back. Numbers Focus step 0 / 9 Press Next . The picture changes at every step. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · try 1 and 2 Main.java a / b ? a % b ? console The one idea int divided by int gives an int. Java keeps the whole groups and throws the leftover away. It cuts, it never rounds, so 10 / 3 is 3 and 1 / 2 is 0. % gives you the leftover that / dropped: 10 % 3 is 1. Make both sides double and the leftover counts as a fraction of a group instead.

title: Pre and Post Increment
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-2 · Pre/post increment and decrement Pre and Post Increment With y = x++ y gets the old value, with y = ++x y gets the new one. Pick the statement Focus copy of the value x · int 5 was 5 y · int no value read x: 5 +1 5 press Next step 0 / 5 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · Run one, then the other. Main.java y gets ? x ends at ? console The one idea Both x++ and ++x add 1 to x. The position of ++ decides what y gets: after x, y gets the value before the increment (5); before x, y gets the value after it (6). x-- and --x work the same way, subtracting 1.

title: Widening, Narrowing, Casting
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-2 · Literals are typed, widening, narrowing, casting Widening, Narrowing, Casting A value moves into a bigger type on its own, but into a smaller one only with a cast, and whatever does not fit is lost. Pick an example Focus Each type is a cup. Bigger cup, wider range of values step 0 / 6 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next Main.java from ? to ? Output console The one idea Java widens for free; narrowing needs a cast and you own whatever is lost. Along byte, short, int, long, float, double, moving right is automatic. Moving left does not compile until you write the cast, and then Java drops digits ( 123.4567890123 becomes 123.45679 ), cuts decimals ( (int) 9.99 is 9) or wraps around ( (int) 3000000000L is -1294967296), with no error and no warning.

title: printf Format Specifiers
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-3 · Formatting output printf Format Specifiers Each % placeholder takes the next argument, in order, and the letters after the % say how that value is written. Pick a printf line Focus Placeholders and arguments, matched in order The line printf builds step 0 / 6 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · dots in the output are spaces added to reach the width. Try the width line. Main.java placeholder ? takes argument ? console The one idea Placeholders are filled left to right from the arguments: the 1st % takes the 1st argument, the 2nd takes the 2nd. The letter after % says how to format the value: s text, d whole number, f decimal. A number before it sets the width (a minus means left aligned), .2 sets two decimals, a comma groups digits, and %n ends the line.

title: Scanner Methods
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-3 · Reading input with Scanner Scanner Methods Each Scanner method takes a different piece of the typed line: one word, the whole line, or one number. What the learner types Focus method next() Run next() nextLine() nextInt() nextDouble() all four each method runs alone on a fresh copy of the typed line · try 42 apples, then nextInt() The one line that runs taken ? still in the line ? console The one idea next() stops at a space , so it takes one word. nextLine() takes everything to the end of the line , spaces included. nextInt() only accepts a whole number and throws InputMismatchException otherwise; nextDouble() takes a number with or without a decimal point.

text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 3-3 · Buffered input and line separators Scanner Buffer nextInt() takes the digits and leaves the line separator behind, so the next nextLine() returns an empty String without waiting. The input buffer · one cell per character Focus Variables read now skipped as whitespace \n = ENTER (line separator) faded = already used step 0 / 0 Press Step to start the program, or Run to watch it play. Another nextInt() skips it, but nextLine() reads up to it, finds nothing, and returns "". When you read a number and then a line, consume the leftover first with an extra myScanner.nextLine() .

title: if / else Path
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 4-1 and 4-3 · if, else if, else, and the conditional operator if / else Path Java checks the conditions top to bottom, runs the block of the first one that is true, and skips the rest. The age the user typed Focus step 0 / 5 ← Back Next → Reset space = next · Try 15: it is also under 65. Main.java age ? price ? console The one idea Java checks the conditions in order, runs the first true one, and skips the rest , even a later condition that would also be true. else has no condition: it catches whatever is left. cond ? a : b is the same choice written as a value : double price = (age < 18) ? 22.50 : 25.00;

title: Logical Operators
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 4-1 · Logical operators Logical Operators Java reads the condition left to right and stops as soon as the answer is known. Pick the values Focus How Java reads the condition left ? not checked right ? whole condition ? if block else block step 0 / 7 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · Try age 12, then age 30. Main.java left side ? right side ? console The one idea && needs both sides true, || needs one, ! flips true and false. Java reads left to right and stops as soon as the answer is known : a false left side settles an && , a true left side settles an || , and the right side is never checked.

title: == vs .equals
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 4-1 · Comparing Strings == vs .equals == checks whether two arrows point at the same object; .equals checks whether the characters match. Where do the two Strings come from? Focus step 0 / 5 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · Try two literals. Main.java name == expected ? .equals ? console The one idea == asks "same object?", .equals asks "same characters?" Text the user types is a new object, so == against a literal is false even when the words match. Two identical literals share one pooled object, which is why == sometimes seems to work. For text you almost always mean .equals , or .equalsIgnoreCase when capital letters should not matter.

title: Method Signature
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 4-2 · Static methods Method Signature It says what you must pass, in what order, and what you get back, and every call has to match it. Pick a method Focus Main.java, inside class Main step 0 / 8 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · Try greetUser for void. You must pass ? You get back ? The one idea The header is a contract. The parameter list says what you must pass and in what order: each argument must have its parameter's type, and the names do not have to match. The return type says what comes back and what you can store it in; void means nothing comes back.

title: Method Call Stack
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 4-2 · Static methods Method Call Stack Java builds a new box, runs the method there, then throws the box away. Step through it and watch the boxes stack up and come down. The call stack Focus nothing running yet step 0 / 0 Press Step to start the program, or Run to watch it play. Step → Run ← Back Reset Experiment: change num1 inside addNumbers space = step · the experiment adds a line that writes to the parameter. Does main's firstNumber change? Main.java Inputs · what main starts with main's variables firstNumber secondNumber firstName lastName Edit while stopped. The run below is computed from these, not replayed. frames on stack ? deepest so far ? console The one idea Every call gets its own frame with its own copies of the values. Parameters are copies, not links: changing num1 inside addNumbers leaves firstNumber in main untouched. The only thing that comes back is the return value, and the frame is gone the moment it returns.

title: Repeated Code to One Method
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 4-2 · Why methods Repeated Code to One Method Pull the repeated lines into one method, turn the numbers into parameters, and call it: main gets shorter, and a fix in one place reaches every call. The program so far Focus Main.java Output console step 0 / 8 Press Next to start. The code and the console change at every step. ← Back Next → Reset space = next · fixed sizes instead of Scanner input. lines in main ? copies of the code ? The one idea Write it once, name it, call it. When the same lines show up again and again, move them into a method, turn the values that change into parameters, and replace each copy with a call. main reads like a list of what happens, and a change in one place reaches every call . The workbook calls this D.R.Y.: Don't Repeat Yourself.

title: One Scanner, Three Ways
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 4-2 · Using a Scanner in multiple methods One Scanner, Three Ways Three ways to let methods read the keyboard. Same program, same output; only where the Scanner lives changes. The third wins. Pick a way Focus way 3 / 3 click a column · 1, 2, 3 on the keyboard ScannerAsParameter.java Scanner objects doAdd says it reads input verdict The one idea One Scanner per program, created in main, handed to each method as a parameter. A static field also gives one object, but hides who reads input and lets one close() cut everyone off. A Scanner per method gives several objects on one keyboard, and what one reads ahead the others never see.

title: switch, Both Forms
text: ← Week 1 index Workbook 1c · Section 4-3 · The switch statement switch, Both Forms In the traditional form it keeps running until it hits a break ; in the arrow form it runs one branch and stops. Pick a version Focus Traditional case 3: Arrow case 3 -> step 0 / 6 ← Back Next → Reset space = next · the day-of-week switch, with the learner typing 3. Try the break removed. dayNumber ? dayName ? console The one idea Both forms jump straight to the case that matches, and default catches every value no case names. The traditional form keeps running down the cases until it reaches a break , so a missing break lets the next case run too. The arrow form runs only its own branch and stops: no break, no fall-through.

Ask the customer whether they want color and how many pages they need. Print the total cost, with two decimals . Data (the nouns) Plan (the verbs, in order) step 0 / 9 Press Next to start. ← Back Next → Reset space = next Main.java console The one idea Before you type, underline the nouns and the verbs. The nouns are your data: inputs become Scanner reads, outputs become printf, fixed values become numbers in the code. The verbs are your steps, in order; a step that depends on an answer is an if/else, and a calculation with a name is a method. The code follows the plan.

title: Thinking in Objects
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 1-1 Thinking in Objects A bike shop has three things in it. Tap each one and see it as an object. The Bike Shop Bike tap object · Bike bike knows frameSize 54 cm price $650.00 does shiftGear() changes gear Mechanic tap object · Mechanic mechanic knows name "Dana" yearsOfExperience 6 does repair(bike) fixes a bike Customer tap object · Customer customer knows name "Sam" budget $800.00 does pay(amount) pays for a bike Three things in the shop. Each one knows something and does something. Tap one. Reset The one idea Look at the world as things that know and do. What a thing knows becomes its fields, what it does becomes its methods. Object Oriented Programming models software on the world around it, one object per thing.

title: One Object, One Job
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 1-2 · Specialization and Responsibilities One Object, One Job A bike shop has three specialists. Give each job to the one who owns it. responsibilities · drag one onto an object, or tap it then tap the object object · the thing sold Bike knows does object · the repair specialist Mechanic knows does object · the money specialist Register knows does Six responsibilities, three objects. Each one is something an object knows or something it does . Reset The one idea Each object owns its own responsibilities. A responsibility is something the object knows (data) or does (an action), and it lives with the specialist it belongs to, so there is one place to look for it. The Register asks the Bike for its price; it does not keep its own copy.

title: Encapsulation
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-1 Encapsulation The fields are locked inside. Try to reach in, then use the door. outside the class main p1.firstName reach in and read the field directly what main is holding value outside · inside private public · the door getFirstName() getAge() setAge(int) object p1 · Person p1 private fields private String firstName "Raymond" private String lastName "Maroun" private int age 35 p1.firstName p1 is a Person. Its three fields are private : main stands outside the box and can only use the door. Reset The one idea Private fields, public door. Mark the fields private so no code outside the class can touch them, then give the class public getters to read them and setters to change them. The compiler holds the lock: p1.firstName in main does not compile, p1.getFirstName() does.

title: The Constructor
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-1 · Instantiating an Object The Constructor Type three arguments, press new, and watch the constructor fill the object. class · the blueprint Person String firstName String lastName int age int energy the constructor call new Person( , , ) new Person(...) → new No objects yet. Press new on the blueprint. The blueprint holds no values . The three boxes are the arguments the constructor will receive. Reset The one idea new makes the object, the constructor fills it. The arguments arrive as parameters, and this.age = age copies each one into the field of the object being built. A field with no parameter, like energy, gets the value the constructor gives it.

title: Derived Getters
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-1 Derived Getters Press getFullName(), change a name, press it again. object · Person person1 String firstName String lastName String fullName no such field getters .getFirstName() .getFullName() → return returned value Nothing returned yet. person1 stores two names. There is no fullName on the card. Reset The one idea A derived getter computes its value from fields each time you call it. getFullName() joins firstName and lastName , so it can never be out of date, and a fullName field would only store the same thing twice.

title: Boolean Getters
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-1 Boolean Getters Pick a field and watch IntelliJ name its getter and setter. class · Person fields click one, then read the right side String firstName get int age get double price get boolean learner is boolean occupied is boolean isDirty is, already IntelliJ · what it generates Alt + Insert or Cmd + N → Getter and Setter getter pick a field setter pick a field The rule IntelliJ follows: the getter starts with get for every type except boolean, where it starts with is . The setter always starts with set . You never type these names; you only name the field. Click a field on the left. The names come from the field name and its type, nothing else. Reset The one idea A boolean field gets an is getter, every other field gets a get getter, and the setter is always set . Name the field without is ( learner , not isLearner ) and let IntelliJ generate the rest.

title: Default Access
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-1 · Default access modifier Default Access Change the modifier on one method, then try to call it from two classes. package com.pluralsight public class Person no modifier String getFirstName() class · same package Main person1.getFirstName() package com.other class · other package Report import com.pluralsight.Person; person1.getFirstName() No modifier means package-private : every class in com.pluralsight can call it, nothing outside. String getFirstName() { return firstName; } Reset The one idea No modifier is not public. Java gives the member package-private access: classes in the same package can use it, classes in any other package cannot. In this course every field and method gets an explicit modifier, so nobody has to guess.

title: Methods Change State
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-2 Methods Change State One Person, two methods. Press them and watch its own energy move. object · Person person2 firstName "Potato" lastName "Sensei" age 33 energy 100 .work() .eat() 100 energy -100 0 100 200 The constructor set person2’s energy to 100 . Press a method on the card. Reset The one idea A method works on the object's own fields. work() and eat() change this.energy , so the change stays in the object. Neither method checks the value: a floor or a cap would be an if you add inside it.

title: Cohesion
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-2 · Encapsulation and Cohesion Cohesion One class does everything. Move each method to the class it belongs in. one class · low cohesion OfficeMachine 6 methods, 3 unrelated jobs show before and after → class Printer class MailClient class CoffeeMaker Six methods, three jobs, one class. Tap a method , then tap the class it belongs in, or drag it there. Reset The one idea A class should hold only what belongs together. When every method in a class works on the same job, the class has high cohesion and changes for one reason. A class that does everything has low cohesion: a change to one job means opening the class that also runs the other two.

title: Method Overloading
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-3 Method Overloading One name, five doors. Drop arguments into the call and see which door opens. class · five constructors, one name Person the call No object yet. Press the green door. Reset The one idea Overloading means one name with different parameter lists. The signature is the name plus the type of each parameter, in order, so Person(int, String) and Person(String, int) are different. The compiler looks at the arguments you pass and picks the one version that matches. If none matches, the code does not compile.

title: The Testing Pyramid
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 3-1 · Types of Software Testing The Testing Pyramid Tap a level of the pyramid, then change one line of code. End-to-End 5 tests screen Ride Scooter database a rider taps Unlock , rides, sees the fare Integration 40 tests screen Ride Scooter database the Ride asks the Scooter getBattery() Unit 200 tests screen Ride Scooter database one Scooter, alone: unlock() , is it unlocked? Scooter.java line 12 change one line of code one test at this level tap a band how many you write few many how fast one runs slow fast how costly to set up cheap costly An app that rents scooters , and its automated tests. Each dot is one test, stacked by level. Reset The one idea Many unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests on top. The bottom is fast and cheap, the top is slow and needs setup. Every change re-runs every test, so the shape keeps the wait short. By hand, a tester would repeat every check after every change.

title: Arrange, Act, Assert
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 3-2 · Parts of a unit test Arrange, Act, Assert One test, three steps. Run them in order, then change what you expect. @Test accelerate_NormalSpeedChange_SpeedIncreased() not run Arrange Set up the object under test. new Car() Act Call the one method being tested. .accelerate(10) Assert Check the result: expected first, actual second. assertEquals expected ? actual - No car yet. Press new Car() in Arrange. One test with three stages . Nothing is set up yet, so there is no car to test. Reset The one idea Arrange sets up, Act calls the one method under test, Assert compares expected with actual. When they match the test passes. When they do not, JUnit fails it and tells you both values, so a wrong expectation or a wrong method is caught at once.

title: Why Doubles Drift
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 4-1 Why Doubles Drift One coin, two tills. Drop ten cents at a time and watch which total stays exact. 10¢ add ten cents till 1 · stored in binary double total prints 0.0 till 2 · exact decimal BigDecimal total prints 0 Two tills, both at zero. Each press drops ten cents into both at once. Reset built from a double new BigDecimal(0.1) prints built from a String new BigDecimal("0.1") prints Two ways to build one tenth. Press each and compare what prints. The one idea A double is stored in binary, so 0.1 is only an approximation and the error grows as you add. A BigDecimal built from a String holds the decimal exactly, so money adds up to the cent. Never build one from a double: it copies the approximation.

title: BigDecimal Operations
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 4-1 · BigDecimal BigDecimal Operations Press a button on the cart total and watch where each answer goes. BigDecimal cartTotal · the variable 0 scale 0 .add(keyboard) 49.99 .add(mouse) 19.99 .add(cable) 7.50 .subtract(coupon) 5.00 .multiply(1.075) 7.5% tax .setScale(2, HALF_UP) round to cents .add(keyboard) without assigning no cartTotal = ← cartTotal = new objects · what each call returns Nothing returned yet. Every call builds a new BigDecimal here. cartTotal holds 0 , BigDecimal.ZERO. Each button asks it for a result. Reset The one idea A BigDecimal never changes: add, subtract, multiply and setScale each return a new one, so write cartTotal = cartTotal.add(price); Multiply grows the scale, setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP) brings it back to cents. Compare with compareTo , never == or equals , and give divide a scale and a rounding mode too.

title: What Static Means
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 4-2 · Introduction to Static What Static Means Some things belong to each player. Some belong to the team. Add players and look at both. look at jersey number team name the team · there is one, and it was there first Team Falcons team name add a player remove a player The team exists before anyone joins. A jersey number cannot: nobody is wearing one yet. Add a player. Reset The one idea A jersey number belongs to one player: every player has their own, and with no players there are none. The team name belongs to the team: there is exactly one, it exists before any player joins, and every player shares it. In Java, a thing that belongs to the whole class instead of to each object is called static . One copy, shared, there from the start.

title: Instance vs Static
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 4-2 Instance vs Static Each object keeps its own name. The school lives once, on the class. Change both. class · the blueprint Learner instance: one per object String name int grade new Learner("Carol", 11) static: one copy, on the class Learner.changeSchool(...) the only copy static String schoolName "Greenwood High" Reset The one idea An instance field lives in every object; a static field lives once, on the class. Changing one object's name touches that object only. Changing the static school through Learner.changeSchool(...) needs no object, and every Learner, old or new, sees the same single value.

title: Utility Classes
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 4-2 · Static classes Utility Classes Open the Math class you have used since week 1. Try to use it two ways. inside the JDK · what a utility class looks like class Math public final class Math { private Math() { } private constructor public static final double PI = 3.14159... static public static long round(double a) static public static double pow(double a, double b) static public static double sqrt(double a) static // ... more static methods, no instance fields at all } class Main · two ways to use it Math.round(12.8) call it on the class name new Math() try to build an object ? your exercise · same shape public class NameFormatter { private NameFormatter() { } private public static String format(...) static } Two things make a utility class: a private constructor and only static members . Press a button to see why. Reset The one idea A utility class is never instantiated: its constructor is private, and everything in it is static, so you call it on the class name. Math.round(12.8) works, new Math() does not compile. Your NameFormatter is built the same way.

title: Has-A
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 5-1 · Class relationships Has-A Three classes and their attributes. Give one class an attribute whose type is another class, and watch what changes. Deck class attribute type size number nothing else yet Card class attribute type suit text value text face up yes or no Hand class attribute type size number nothing else yet add a Deck has cards a Hand has cards probe take Card away take Deck away Reset Every attribute here has a built-in type: number , text , yes or no . That is all you have used so far. Press a Deck has cards . The one idea A has-a relationship is an attribute whose type is another class. A Deck has cards, so Deck holds Card and depends on it. A Hand has cards, the same way. Card gains nothing and knows nothing: the dependency runs one way, from the holder to the held.

title: Know vs Do Sorter
desc: A sentence about an object: is it something it knows (a field) or something it does (a method)?
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Module 1 · Game Know vs Do Sorter An object has two kinds of responsibility: what it knows and what it does. Sort sixteen of them. KNOW = a piece of data the object stores, the brains · DO = an action the object performs, the muscle · most objects do both The one idea Something an object knows becomes a field; something it does becomes a method. title: Derived or Stored?
desc: A getter name and a class: does it read a field or compute a value?

Keys S and D answer. stored = there is a field with that name, the getter returns it · derived = no such field, the value is calculated from other fields The one idea A getter does not need a field of its own. If a value can be worked out from fields the object already has, like a full name from a first and last name, compute it in the getter instead of storing it twice. The caller cannot tell the difference.

title: Overload Matcher

text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 2-3 · Game Overload Matcher Three versions of one method and one call. Pick the version Java runs, or say it does not compile. Fifteen rounds. Press the version that runs (keys 1, 2, 3), or does not compile (key 4) when none fits or two fit equally well. Start Round over Play again round 0 / 15 Press Start or Enter. Keys 1 to 4 answer. Java matches the argument types in order · an exact match wins · an int can widen to a double, a double never becomes an int · a String never converts · two equal fits = ambiguous The one idea Java picks an overload by the types of the arguments, in order, before the program runs. An exact match wins; an int may widen to a double when nothing matches exactly; a String never turns into a number. No fit, or two equally good fits, and the call does not compile.

title: Pyramid Climber
desc: A test described in one line: unit, integration or end to end?
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 3-1 · Game Pyramid Climber Every automated test sits on one level of the testing pyramid. Name the level of fifteen tests and climb. Every right answer climbs one level. Start Climb over Play again round 0 / 15 Press Start . Keys U, I and E answer. UNIT = the methods of one object · INTEGRATION = objects or sub-systems working together · END-TO-END = the full experience of a user The one idea Ask how much of the system the test touches. One object's methods is a Unit test: fast, and most of your tests. Objects or sub-systems talking to each other, such as a real database or file, is an Integration test: slower, fewer. A user's whole path through the app is an End-to-End test: the most setup, the fewest tests, at the top.

Pick the one that matches the check: equal values with expected first, a true or false condition, null or not null, or an exception thrown by a call wrapped in a lambda. The right one fails for the right reason and prints a message you can read.

title: Exact or Drift?
desc: A money calculation in double or BigDecimal: type what prints.
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 4-1 · Game Exact or Drift? A money calculation in double or in BigDecimal. Say exactly what prints. Twelve rounds. When the output is long, pick it from four with keys 1 to 4. Start Round over Play again round 0 / 12 Press Start . Enter submits a typed answer, keys 1 to 4 pick one. double = binary, most decimals are close, not exact · BigDecimal from a String = exact, keeps its decimal places · every BigDecimal method returns a new object The one idea A double stores the nearest binary value, so cents drift; a BigDecimal built from a String stores the decimal exactly. Build it from a String, assign every result ( total = total.add(price); ), round with setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP) , and compare with compareTo , never equals .

title: Static or Instance?
desc: A member described in one line: static or instance, and can you call it without an object?
text: ← Week 5 index Workbook 4a · Section 4-2 · Game Static or Instance? A static member belongs to the class; an instance member belongs to one object. Sort fifteen of them. Game static or instance? score 0 time 0.0s Static or Instance? Each round is a member described in one line, or a one-line call. Press S if it belongs to the class (no object needed), I if it belongs to one object (you need an object to reach it). Start Round over Play again round 0 / 15 Press Start . Keys S and I answer. STATIC = one copy for the whole class, called on the class name · INSTANCE = one copy per object, called on a variable · ask: does it need one object's data? The one idea Ask whether the member needs one particular object's data. If it does (this learner's name, this account's balance), it is an instance member and you reach it through an object: alice.printDetails() . If it does not (a value everyone shares, a calculation that only needs its inputs), it is static and you reach it through the class: Learner.changeSchool("Lakeside Academy") , Math.sqrt(25) .

The class that needs the other one holds it: one object when there is exactly one, an ArrayList when there can be many. The relationship goes one way: the owned class does not need to know who holds it.

title: The Duplication Problem
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 1-1 The Duplication Problem Two classes, some lines written twice. Tap what repeats. Animal class nothing written here yet Cat class name age eat() meow() Dog class name age eat() bark() Cat and Dog each have four members, and three of them are the same in both. Tap one that appears twice. Reset The one idea What two classes share is written once, in a parent class. Each child keeps only what makes it different and inherits the rest. Pulling the shared part up is called generalization, and it is how code stays D.R.Y.: one place to change, not two.

title: Is-A
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 1-1 Is-A Say the sentence out loud. Pick a pair, then flip it. flip the pair Reset The one idea Inheritance is an is-a relationship, and it only reads one way. If "a Dog is an Animal" sounds true, Dog can extend Animal, and the arrow points from the child to the parent. If the sentence only works with "has a", that is an attribute, not inheritance.

title: Reading a Class Diagram
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 1-1 Reading a Class Diagram Two classes, drawn the way developers sketch them. Tap any part. This is a class diagram: one box per class, three bands in each box, and one arrow between them. Tap a band, a sign, a name, a type, or the arrow. Reset The one idea A class box has three bands: the name, the attributes, the methods. The sign in front says who can reach a member: minus private, plus public, hash protected. The type comes after the colon. The hollow triangle always points at the parent. You will draw these same boxes yourself in diagrams.net.

title: What a Child Inherits
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 1-2 What a Child Inherits Call a method on the dog and watch which class answers. object · built with new Dog() dog comes from Animal name "Lucky" age 15 added by Dog breed "Doberman" dog.setName("Potato") dog.getAge() dog.getBreed() class · the parent Animal String name int age setName(String name) getAge() Dog extends Animal class · the child Dog String breed getBreed() setBreed(String breed) Dog writes only breed and its two methods. Everything in Animal comes along with extends . Reset The one idea A child class has everything its parent has, without writing it again. When you call a method on a Dog, Java looks in Dog first, then up in Animal. The Dog object carries the Animal fields too, plus the ones Dog adds.

title: Private, Protected, Public
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 1-2 Private, Protected, Public Pick who is knocking, then try each of Animal's three doors. package com.pluralsight public class Animal code inside Animal private String name door protected String favoriteFood door public String getName() door class · same package Dog extends Animal: a child class · same package Main not a child package com.other class · other package Kennel not a child Animal has three members, one per modifier. Four classes would like to use them. Reset The one idea private opens for the class itself only. protected opens for the class, its children, and every class in the same package. public opens for everyone. A child inherits a private field but cannot touch it: it goes through the getter.

title: The Constructor Chain
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 1-3 The Constructor Chain Build one dog, one line per press, and see which constructor prints first. Dog dog = new Dog(); press to start building printed, in this order 1 2 constructor · in the parent Animal() println "I am in the Animal Empty Constructor" Dog extends Animal constructor · in the child Dog() super(); first line; Java adds it if you leave it out println "I am in the Dog Empty Constructor" Each constructor prints one line. Nothing has run yet : which line do you expect first? Reset The one idea Parent first, child after. new Dog() enters Dog's constructor, but its first line is super() , so Animal's constructor body runs to the end before Dog's own lines do. A dog is an animal first: that part is built first.

title: super With Arguments
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 1-3 super With Arguments Tap an argument and follow it: up to Animal, or kept by Dog. the statement new Dog( "Lucky" , 15 , "Doberman" ); object · the dog being built Animal's fields name empty age empty Dog's field breed empty constructor · in the parent Animal( String name , int age ) this.name = name; this.age = age; super(...) carries arguments up constructor · in the child Dog( String name , int age , String breed ) super ( name , age ); first statement this.breed = breed ; move super(...) down one line Three arguments go into new Dog(...) , but Dog has only one field of its own. The other two belong to Animal. Reset The one idea The arguments named in super(...) go up to the parent's constructor; the child stores the rest. Dog cannot store name and age itself, they are private in Animal, so it hands them up. And super(...) is always the first statement: the parent part is built before the child does anything of its own.

title: Method Overriding
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-1 · Overriding methods Method Overriding Call eat() on each object. Then remove a child's version and call again. class · the parent Human eat() "I am a Human and I am Hungry!" new object · Human human human.eat() class · extends Human Caveman eat() remove new object · Caveman caveman caveman.eat() class · extends Human ModernPerson eat() remove new object · ModernPerson modernPerson modernPerson.eat() Reset The one idea Overriding replaces an inherited method with the child's own version. Same name, same parameters, new body. When eat() is called, Java starts at the object's own class and uses the first eat() it finds on the way up to the parent.

title: The @Override Annotation
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-1 · @Override annotation The @Override Annotation Misspell the method, call it, then switch @Override on. class · the parent Human eat() remove it "I am a Human and I am Hungry!" class · extends Human Caveman eat() inherited from Human, unchanged + @Override eat() misspell it "Me Hunt Lion and Eat!" object · Caveman caveman caveman.eat() Reset The one idea @Override asks the compiler to check your override. Without it, a misspelled name quietly becomes a new method, and a method removed or renamed in the parent leaves yours overriding nothing. With it, both mistakes are a compile error you see at once. Write it on every override.

title: Variable, Type, Object
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-1 · Polymorphism Variable, Type, Object One statement, three things. Tap each part, then change either side. variable type variable = object ; variable type · the label Human Caveman ModernPerson variable · the box → ✕ object · its real class create a different object new Human() new Caveman() new ModernPerson() Reset The one idea The variable type is fixed, and it is what the compiler checks. The object keeps its own class. A variable of the parent type can refer to any child object: Human h accepts a Human, a Caveman or a ModernPerson. Never the other way around: a Caveman variable cannot refer to a plain Human.

title: Base Class References
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-1 · Base class references Base Class References One Human variable, two kinds of object. Try both calls on each. variable · its type is Human Human h call a method through h h.eat() h.run() put an object in h h = new Human() h = new Caveman() → ✕ refers to object · its real class Caveman eat() run() "Me running away from dinosaur!" Reset The one idea The variable's type decides what you may call. The object decides what runs. The compiler only sees Human h , so only Human's methods are allowed. At run time Java looks at the real object, and a Caveman answers eat() the Caveman way.

title: A Parent-Type Parameter
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-1 · Polymorphism A Parent-Type Parameter One method, one Human slot. Pass each object in and see what it takes. → ✕ pass it in method · written once feed(String label, Human human ) the parameter Human human what the method does with it human.eat() Reset The one idea A parameter is a variable of the parent type. Anything that is a Human fits in Human human , so one feed method serves every child, even a child written later. The method only says human.eat() , and the object decides which eat() runs .

title: One List, Many Types
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-1 · Polymorphism One List, Many Types One list, three kinds of Human. Ask each one to eat, one press at a time. List<Human> people size 3 people.get(0).eat() Reset The one idea A list typed with the parent class can hold any of its children. A List<Human> takes a Human, a Caveman and a ModernPerson, because each one is a Human. The loop makes the same call on every element, and each object answers with the eat() of its own class .

title: instanceof and Downcasting
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-1 · Polymorphism instanceof and Downcasting Ask each object if it is a Caveman. Then cast it and see what Java does. Reset The one idea Test first, then cast. A Human variable only reaches what Human has. instanceof asks the object what it really is, and a downcast such as (Caveman) person gives you a Caveman variable for the same object, so run() opens up. Cast an object that is not a Caveman and the program stops with ClassCastException .

title: Abstract Classes
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-2 · Abstraction Abstract Classes Try to build an Asset. Then build a House and look at what it carries. abstract class Asset fields String description int yearAcquired BigDecimal originalCost constructor Asset(...) fills the three fields finished method printMessage() new Asset(...) → new No Asset object. ↑ extends class · extends Asset House its own fields String address int squareFeet int lotSize new House(...) → new No House object yet. Reset The one idea An abstract class is a parent too general to build. It is a real class: it holds fields, constructors and finished methods for its children to inherit. But new Asset(...) does not compile, because nobody owns just "an asset". You build a concrete child such as House , and every House is still an Asset.

title: Abstract Methods
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 2-2 · Abstraction Abstract Methods Asset leaves a blank. Fill it in House, call it, then take it out again. abstract class Asset finished methods getDescription() has a body getYearAcquired() has a body abstract method BigDecimal getValue() no body ← extends does not compile class · extends Asset House a house to try int squareFeet int lotSize the blank from Asset BigDecimal getValue() missing write getValue() house.getValue() getValue() returns Reset The one idea An abstract method is a blank the parent leaves for its children. Asset writes the signature of getValue() and no body. Every concrete child must override it, or that child does not compile. In return, any Asset you ever hold is sure to have a getValue() you can call.

title: Is-A or Has-A
desc: Two things appear: decide whether one IS a kind of the other, HAS the other, or neither.
text: ← Week 6 index Workbook 5a · Section 1-1 · Game Is-A or Has-A? Two things appear. Does the first one IS-A kind of the second, HAS the second inside it, or neither? Fifteen rounds. Game is-a or has-a? score 0 time 0.0s Is-A or Has-A? Each round shows two class names. Say the sentence in your head: "A is a B" or "A has a B". Press 1 for IS-A, 2 for HAS-A, 3 for neither. Start Round over Play again round 0 / 15 Press Start or Enter. Restart Enter or Space skips the wait after an answer. IS-A = the child extends the parent · HAS-A = one class keeps the other in a field · is-a only works one way · neither = they have nothing to do with each other The one idea Say the sentence out loud. If "a Dog is an Animal" is true, Dog extends Animal. If "a Phone is a Battery" is false but "a Phone has a Battery" is true, Battery is a field inside Phone. title: Comparable
text: ← Week 7 index Workbook 6a · Section 2-2 Comparable Tap two songs to compare them, then let sort() do the same thing. songs · a List<Song>, in list order Collections.sort(songs) the question a.compareTo(b) Song answers with: this.seconds - other.seconds ? a negative number a goes before b zero same place a positive number a goes after b Reset The one idea Comparable is one promise: compareTo. It answers with a negative number, zero or a positive number, meaning before, same place or after. title: Where a Lambda Comes From
text: ← Week 7 index Workbook 6a · Section 4-2 · Lambda Expressions Where a Lambda Comes From Start from a method you know. Remove what Java can work out, one piece per press. hand it an employee · tap one Reset The one idea A lambda is a method with everything removed that Java can work out by itself. What is left is the parameter, an arrow and the body. It takes the same input and gives the same answer as the method did. It has no name, so you never call it yourself: you hand it to a method such as filter or forEach , and that method calls it.

title: From the Loop to the Stream
text: ← Week 7 index Workbook 6a · Section 4-2 · Lambda Expressions From the Loop to the Stream The same search twice: carried by hand in a loop, then flowing through a pipeline. The loop you take each employee, test it and add it yourself Next pass the list for (Employee employee : employees) the test if ( employee.getAge() < 40 ) if the new list matchingEmployees.add(employee); The stream the data flows through a pipeline, you write only the test Run the stream source · data at rest employees.stream() transformation · data in transit .filter(employee -> employee.getAge() < 40 ) filter destination · data at rest .toList() Print the new list fill the new list first, with the loop or the stream above The loop that prints Next pass for (Employee matchingEmployee : matchingEmployees) { System.out.println(matchingEmployee); } println forEach Run forEach matchingEmployees.forEach(matchingEmployee -> System.out.println(matchingEmployee) ); forEach Reset The one idea A stream is a pipeline. The data leaves the source and the work happens while it travels: here filter , with your lambda as the test. toList takes what reaches the end and saves it in a new list, the destination. Game run the lambda score 0 time 0.0s Lambda Lab Read the lambda: parameter, arrow, body. The stream hands it the input shown. Work out what comes back, or what is printed, and pick it. Start Round over Play again round 0 / 14 Press Start or Enter. Restart Enter or Space skips the wait after an answer. parameter -> body · the body is an expression whose value is returned · a block body in braces needs return · two parameters go in parentheses The one idea A lambda is a method without a name: parameters on the left of the arrow, the body on the right. A stream calls it once for each element, handing the element in as the parameter. An expression body is returned as it is; a block body in braces must say return .

title: Stream Predictor
desc: A list and a stream pipeline: predict the result.
text: ← Week 7 index Workbook 6a · Section 4-3 · Game Stream Predictor A list and a stream pipeline. Predict what it prints. Sixteen rounds. Game source, steps, result score 0 time 0.0s Stream Predictor Read the list, then follow the pipeline step by step from the top. Pick what the last line prints. A pipeline never changes the original list. Start Round over Play again round 0 / 16 Press Start or Enter. Restart Enter or Space skips the wait after an answer. filter keeps the elements that pass · map changes each element · distinct drops repeats · sorted orders · count and reduce end the stream with a value · each step receives what the step before sent The one idea A stream is a source, a few steps, and an end. Each step receives only what the step before it sent on: filter keeps fewer, map changes each one, distinct drops repeats. The end gives the result, and the original list is left as it was.

title: Bug Hunter 7
desc: Short snippets with interfaces, generics and streams, one bug each: tap the line that breaks it.
text: ← Week 7 index Workbook 6a · Game Bug Hunter 7 A short program with interfaces, generics or streams and one bug. Tap the line that breaks it. Twelve rounds. Game find the bug score 0 time 0.0s Bug Hunter 7 Each snippet has exactly one bug. Read it, then tap the line the compiler or the JVM complains about. Start Round over Play again round 0 / 12 Press Start or Enter. Restart Enter or Space skips the wait after an answer. a class must write every abstract method of its interface · the variable type decides what you may call · T extends sets a limit · a stream must end in collect, count, reduce or forEach · a lambda may use only effectively final locals The one idea Most bugs here are the compiler keeping a promise you made. An interface promises methods, a generic type promises one kind of value, a bound promises a limit, and a lambda promises not to change the locals it reads. Read the error line first and ask which promise it points at.
